_about: v5: v4 after the lettered judge. Thought balloons no longer read as lowercase fragments, speech keeps to the setting (no modern slang in historical or fantasy scenes), spiked lines keep their content, and the sound-effect guide gives no example words to copy. Sentences start with a capital.

types.think_bubble: a thought balloon (a tail of small circles)
types.spiked_bubble: a balloon ringed by thin spikes
types.standalone_text: lettering on the art, without a balloon
types.background_text: text that is part of the scene

guides.speech_bubble: Ordinary dialogue said aloud to someone in the scene. Write it the way an English speaker of that age and standing would say it in the same situation, with natural contractions and a register that matches how polite, casual or rough the speaker is. Fit the setting: a historical, martial-arts or fantasy world avoids modern slang (gotta, gonna, dude), a modern school or office story may use it. Replace Korean honorific endings with English politeness (sir, please, a softer phrasing) or drop them. Avoid stiff, textbook sentences.
guides.think_bubble: An unspoken thought: the character talking to themselves, reacting, planning or worrying. Write it as inner voice in the first person, the way people think in English: direct and personal, with questions to oneself where the thought asks one. Use full, properly capitalised sentences. Do not address it to the other characters or turn it into narration. An ellipsis is natural where the thought trails off, but do not add one to every line.
guides.cloud_bubble: Light, playful, affectionate or teasing speech, often cute, flirty or happily excited. Make it sound warm and lively in English: friendly word choice, a playful turn of phrase, a soft exclamation where the mood is bright. A tilde (~) only where the line is sing-song in a way English would show. Avoid flat, formal phrasing that loses the playfulness, and do not make it childish.
guides.wiggle_bubble: An unsteady or unnatural voice. Often the speaker is shaken: scared, weak, hurt, embarrassed or unsure. In dark scenes the same outline marks an eerie, ghostly or menacing voice. Choose words that carry that voice: hesitant, trailing phrasing for a shaken speaker; slow, cold, ominous phrasing for an eerie one. A single stutter or broken-off sentence only where the speaker really falters; never stutter every word.
guides.scream_bubble: The line is shouted, cried out or roared: anger, panic, pain, a battle cry or a call across distance. Make it punchy in English: short words, a strong verb or interjection, one or two exclamation marks. Stretch a drawn-out cry or groan the way English comics write it (Nooo!, Ughhh!). Do not soften it into a calm sentence, and do not write it all in capitals: the burst balloon already shows the volume.
guides.spiked_bubble: A sudden jolt: a shocked inner reaction, a flash of anger, a realisation, or a sharp, tense remark. Make it sound immediate in English, the way a gut reaction is said, and keep everything the line says: a threat stays a full threat, a realisation keeps what was realised. Avoid stiff, explanatory phrasing, and do not inflate it into a shout with extra exclamation marks or capitals.
guides.hexagon_bubble: A voice that comes through something: a phone, radio, broadcast, intercom, AI, magic message or telepathy. Keep the speaker's own personality and register as for ordinary dialogue; a machine or announcement speaks in clipped, impersonal, formal English. Do not add sound-effect words or brackets around the line.
guides.square_bubble: A narration or voice-over box: the narrator, a character's voice-over, or a scene or time caption. Write clear, written English as in a novel's narration, in one consistent tense and voice, slightly more formal than dialogue. Short captions such as places, dates or time skips read like English captions (Three days later. / The Imperial Palace). Avoid chatty fillers and spoken interjections.
guides.system_bubble: A game-style system window as in game-fantasy webtoons: notifications, quests, skills, stats, level-ups and warnings. Use the conventions of English game and LitRPG text: clear, concise, consistent terms (Level Up!, Quest Complete, You have acquired [Title].), standard game vocabulary (HP, MP, EXP, Strength) and title-style names for skills, items and quests inside brackets. Keep brackets, numbers and symbols exactly. Avoid literal Korean word order and romanising terms English readers would not understand.
guides.standalone_text: Lettering placed straight on the art without a balloon: short muttered words, an off-panel voice, an aside, a small exclamation, a label, or the chapter credits and notices. Translate it as an English letterer would set such loose text: as short as the original, natural and to the point. Credits use the usual English form (Art by / Story by / Original Story). Do not expand it into a full sentence or add explanations.
guides.background_text: Text inside the scene itself: shop signs, posters, slogans, screens, phone messages, chat windows, books, labels and graffiti. Translate it as that object would read in English: short, signage-like or message-like, in the style of the medium (a sign is a noun phrase, a chat message is casual). Keep it as brief as the original and do not explain it or turn it into dialogue.
guides.title_panel: A series title, chapter title or episode heading, or the credits beside them. Give an English title as a publisher would: concise, in title case, catchy where the original is, keeping wordplay if you can. Translate a title's meaning rather than romanising it; personal names stay names, romanised. Chapter numbers follow English form (Chapter 31).
guides.sfx_sound: A drawn sound effect or action word: an impact, an explosion, a footstep, a swish, a heartbeat, crowd noise, a groan, or an action written as a sound. First decide what is happening in the scene, then give the English comics onomatopoeia or action word an English letterer would draw for exactly that, in capitals and about as long as the original. A long or repeated Korean sound becomes a stretched English one. Never transliterate the Korean syllables and never write a sentence.
